PROFESSIONAL CORPORATION — FORMATION INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Law Corporation

PROFESSIONAL CORPORATION DECLARATION
The name of the corporation is Acme Law Corporation. Acme Law Corporation is a professional corporation within the meaning of the Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act (Cal. Corp. Code § 13400 et seq.), organized under the General Corporation Law to render professional services in the profession of law. The initial street address of Acme Law Corporation is 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105. The name of Acme Law Corporation's initial agent for service of process in California is Jordan Alex Lee. The agent's street address in California is 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105.

PROFESSIONAL CORPORATION DEFINED; MOSCONE-KNOX AS A GENERAL REGULATORY FRAMEWORK
California's Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act (Cal. Corp. Code § 13400 et seq.) is the statute requiring a corporation that renders certain licensed services to organize as a "professional corporation" rather than as an ordinary business corporation. Its structure is a general framework, not a fixed list of named professions written into the Act itself. The Act defines "professional services" generically, by cross-reference to licensure: any service "lawfully rendered only pursuant to a license, certification, or registration authorized by the Business and Professions Code, the Chiropractic Act, or the Osteopathic Act." A "professional corporation" is, in turn, a corporation organized under the General Corporation Law that renders professional services in a single profession pursuant to a currently effective "certificate of registration issued by the governmental agency regulating the profession." That certificate-of-registration mechanism is itself not universal within the Act: the same subsection carves out a specific list of licensing boards — including the Medical Board of California, the Podiatric Medical Board, the Osteopathic Medical Board, the Dental Board, the Dental Hygiene Board, the State Board of Pharmacy, the Veterinary Medical Board, the California Architects Board, the Court Reporters Board, the Board of Behavioral Sciences, the Speech-Language Pathology and Audiology and Hearing Aid Dispensers Board, the Board of Registered Nursing, the State Board of Optometry, and the California Board of Occupational Therapy — whose licensees are not required to obtain a Moscone-Knox certificate of registration at all, because those professions are instead governed by their own separate profession-specific corporation provisions elsewhere in the Business and Professions Code. Professions not on that carve-out list, such as law and public accountancy, do go through the Moscone-Knox certificate-of-registration process, administered by their own regulating agency (for example, the State Bar for a law corporation). Either way, the profession-specific acts layer additional, profession-specific requirements on top of — they do not replace — the Moscone-Knox framework itself.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Professional services” means any type of professional services that may be lawfully rendered only pursuant to a license, certification, or registration authorized by the Business and Professions Code, the Chiropractic Act, or the Osteopathic Act."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 13401(a), Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act, definition of “professional services” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=13401.)
  "“Professional corporation” means a corporation organized under the General Corporation Law or pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 13406 that is engaged in rendering professional services in a single profession, except as otherwise authorized in Section 13401.5, pursuant to a certificate of registration issued by the governmental agency regulating the profession as herein provided and that in its practice or business designates itself as a professional or other corporation as may be required by statute. However, any professional corporation or foreign professional corporation rendering professional services by persons duly licensed by the Medical Board of California or any examining committee under the jurisdiction of the board, the Podiatric Medical Board of California, the Osteopathic Medical Board of California, the Dental Board of California, the Dental Hygiene Board of California, the California State Board of Pharmacy, the Veterinary Medical Board, the California Architects Board, the Court Reporters Board of California, the Board of Behavioral Sciences, the Speech-Language Pathology and Audiology and Hearing Aid Dispensers Board, the Board of Registered Nursing, the State Board of Optometry, or the California Board of Occupational Therapy shall not be required to obtain a certificate of registration in order to render those professional services."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 13401(b), Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act, definition of “professional corporation” and the certificate-of-registration carve-out for enumerated licensing boards (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=13401.)
  Known gap: The two citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 13401, so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones. This description of the certificate-of-registration carve-out is limited to the licensing boards Section 13401(b) itself names as of the version fetched here; it is not a claim that this list is exhaustive of every California licensed profession or that it will remain unchanged. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific kind of entity — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific licensed professional's corporation, and professional-corporation requirements (including which professions must use one, ownership rules, naming rules, and licensing-board oversight) vary by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation, does not itself obtain any certificate of registration or licensing-board approval, and does not determine which state's law, or which profession-specific rules, apply to any specific person's or group's plan to incorporate.

SHARE OWNERSHIP RESTRICTED TO LICENSED PERSONS, WITH A NARROW MINORITY EXCEPTION
California's general rule for a professional corporation's shares is an ownership restriction, not merely a management restriction: shares of capital stock "may be issued only to a licensed person or to a person who is licensed to render the same professional services" in the jurisdiction where that person practices, and "any shares issued in violation of this restriction shall be void." A separate section, Cal. Corp. Code § 13401.5, then supplies a narrow, list-based exception to that rule: for a specifically designated set of professional corporation types — mostly health-care professions, such as a medical corporation, podiatric medical corporation, psychological corporation, nursing corporation, dental corporation, and a number of others enumerated by subdivision (a) through (s) of that section — certain other licensed persons who are not licensed in the corporation's own profession may nonetheless be shareholders, officers, directors, or professional employees, subject to two caps: the shares those other licensed persons collectively hold cannot exceed 49 percent of the total shares, and the number of such shareholders cannot exceed the number of shareholders licensed in the corporation's own profession. This exception is not universal — it applies only to the professional corporation types Section 13401.5 itself designates, and, notably, does not extend to a law corporation or an accountancy corporation, neither of which appears among the designated types.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Subject to the provisions of subdivision (b), shares of capital stock in a professional corporation may be issued only to a licensed person or to a person who is licensed to render the same professional services in the jurisdiction or jurisdictions in which the person practices, and any shares issued in violation of this restriction shall be void."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 13406(a), Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act, restriction of share ownership to licensed persons (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=13406.)
  "Notwithstanding subdivision (d) of Section 13401 and any other provision of law, the following licensed persons may be shareholders, officers, directors, or professional employees of the professional corporations designated in this section so long as the sum of all shares owned by those licensed persons does not exceed 49 percent of the total number of shares of the professional corporation so designated herein, and so long as the number of those licensed persons owning shares in the professional corporation so designated herein does not exceed the number of persons licensed by the governmental agency regulating the designated professional corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 13401.5, Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act, 49-percent minority-ownership exception for designated professional corporation types (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=13401.5.)

PROFESSIONAL CORPORATION NAMING GOVERNED BY PROFESSION-SPECIFIC LAW, NOT ORDINARY CORPORATE NAMING RULES
A professional corporation's permitted name is not fixed by the Moscone-Knox Act's own text the way an ordinary corporation's name is fixed by the General Corporation Law. Instead, Cal. Corp. Code § 13409(a) hands the naming question to whatever law or regulation governs the specific profession: a professional corporation "may adopt any name permitted by a law expressly applicable to the profession in which the corporation is engaged or by a rule or regulation of the governmental agency regulating that profession," and the Secretary of State may require an affidavit establishing that the chosen name complies with that profession-specific law. This means the actual naming rule a given professional corporation must follow — for example, whether it must include a shareholder's surname, the words "Professional Corporation" or an abbreviation such as "P.C." or "Prof. Corp.," or a term describing the type of practice — is set by that profession's own governing law or its regulating board's rules, not by Moscone-Knox itself. Section 13409(a) is also expressly "[s]ubject to Section 201," so a professional corporation's name remains bound by the General Corporation Law's baseline naming rules even after satisfying the profession-specific requirement: the Secretary of State will not accept a name it determines is "likely to mislead the public," and the name must be "distinguishable in the records of the Secretary of State" from other registered and reserved corporate names.

  "Subject to Section 201, a professional corporation may adopt any name permitted by a law expressly applicable to the profession in which the corporation is engaged or by a rule or regulation of the governmental agency regulating that profession."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 13409(a), Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act, naming governed by profession-specific law or regulating-agency rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=13409.)
  "The name of a corporation shall not be a name that the Secretary of State determines is likely to mislead the public and shall be distinguishable in the records of the Secretary of State from all of the following:"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 201(b), General Corporation Law, baseline not-misleading and distinguishable-name requirements (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=201.)

The specific naming requirement for any one profession (for example, whether a surname or a particular abbreviation is required) is set by that profession's own governing law or regulating board's rules, which this clause does not individually verify for every profession — it verifies only the Moscone-Knox and General Corporation Law framework that hands that question to profession-specific law in the first place. INCORPORATION DOES NOT SHIELD A PROFESSIONAL FROM LIABILITY FOR THEIR OWN MALPRACTICE
Neither the Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act nor the profession-specific acts layered on top of it contain an express provision stating that a licensed professional's own liability for their own professional negligence disappears when they incorporate. Forming a professional corporation is understood, under general California corporate and agency principles, to shield a shareholder-professional from personal liability for the corporation's ordinary business debts and, in most circumstances, from liability for the malpractice of other shareholders or employees — but it does not extend that shield to a professional's liability for their own individually negligent or wrongful acts in rendering professional services, which remains a matter of personal responsibility regardless of the corporate form through which the services were rendered. Two profession-specific statutes in the Business and Professions Code supply indirect but real statutory evidence that this liability exposure persists notwithstanding incorporation: both the law corporation article and the accountancy corporation article condition the corporation's certificate of registration on the corporation maintaining insurance or other security for client claims arising out of the rendering of professional services — a mandatory-insurance condition that would serve no purpose if incorporating eliminated the underlying liability the insurance is meant to cover.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "That a law corporation, as a condition of obtaining a certificate pursuant to the Professional Corporation Act and this article, shall provide and maintain security by insurance or otherwise for claims against it by its clients for errors and omissions arising out of the rendering of professional services."
  — Bus. & Prof. Code § 6171(b), Law Corporations article, mandatory insurance or security for client errors-and-omissions claims as a condition of the certificate of registration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=6171.)
  "that an accountancy corporation as a condition of obtaining a certificate pursuant to the Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act and this article shall provide adequate security by insurance or otherwise for claims against it by its clients arising out of the rendering of professional services."
  — Bus. & Prof. Code § 5157(b), Accountancy Corporation article, mandatory security for client claims as a condition of the certificate of registration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=5157.)
  Known gap: This clause differs from the others in this document in kind, not just in citation: unlike Sections 13401, 13401.5, 13406, 13409, 13403, 13404, and 13410, no provision of the Moscone-Knox Act itself was found, in the text verified here, to state in so many words that a professional corporation does not shield a professional from liability for their own malpractice. The rule as stated in the body above rests substantially on general California common-law and agency principles (that an individual remains personally liable for their own tortious conduct regardless of the corporate form through which they act) rather than on a single operative Moscone-Knox statute, and no case law citation establishing this specific rule for professional corporations is included here — case law research for this point was not completed as part of this verification pass, consistent with this document's statutory focus. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted profession-specific statutes, Bus. & Prof. Code § 6171 (law corporations) and Bus. & Prof. Code § 5157 (accountancy corporations), and are used here only as indirect evidence — a mandatory-insurance requirement consistent with continuing personal liability exposure — not as a direct statutory statement of the liability rule itself; they are treated as two independent sources. The mandatory-insurance requirement they state applies, by its own terms, only to law corporations and accountancy corporations specifically, not to every professional corporation type; other professions' corporation acts were not individually checked for an equivalent insurance requirement here. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific kind of entity — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific licensed professional's corporation, and professional-corporation requirements (including which professions must use one, ownership rules, naming rules, and licensing-board oversight) vary by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation, does not itself obtain any certificate of registration or licensing-board approval, and does not determine which state's law, or which profession-specific rules, apply to any specific person's or group's plan to incorporate.

GENERAL CORPORATION LAW APPLIES EXCEPT WHERE MOSCONE-KNOX CONFLICTS
A professional corporation is not governed by an entirely separate corporate-law regime. Cal. Corp. Code § 13403 states the relationship directly: "[t]he provisions of the General Corporation Law shall apply to professional corporations, except where such provisions are in conflict with or inconsistent with the provisions of this part." Consistent with that structure, Cal. Corp. Code § 13404 confirms that a professional corporation is formed the same way an ordinary corporation is formed — "under the General Corporation Law" — for the added purpose of qualifying as a professional corporation, with the one required deviation that its articles of incorporation "shall contain a specific statement that the corporation is a professional corporation within the meaning of this part." So a professional corporation exists on the same General Corporation Law chassis as an ordinary for-profit corporation, modified by the Moscone-Knox Act's own rules only where the two conflict — for example, Section 13403 itself goes on to supply special reduced-director rules for a professional corporation with only one or two shareholders, displacing what the General Corporation Law would otherwise require.

  — Cal. Corp. Code § 13403, Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act, General Corporation Law applies except where conflicting (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=13403.)
  "A corporation may be formed under the General Corporation Law or pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 13406 for the purposes of qualifying as a professional corporation in the manner provided in this part and rendering professional services. The articles of incorporation of a professional corporation shall contain a specific statement that the corporation is a professional corporation within the meaning of this part."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 13404, Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act, formation under the General Corporation Law and the required articles statement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=13404.)

SEPARATE LICENSING BOARD REGISTRATION REQUIRED IN ADDITION TO FILING ARTICLES
Filing articles of incorporation with the California Secretary of State is not, by itself, enough to let a professional corporation render professional services. Cal. Corp. Code § 13410(a) subjects a professional corporation to the applicable rules, regulations, and disciplinary provisions of "the governmental agency regulating the profession in which such corporation is engaged" — the same licensing board that regulates individual practitioners of that profession, layered onto the corporation itself. A concrete, verified example of the two-step process this creates is the law corporation: Bus. & Prof. Code § 6160 defines a "law corporation" as one that "is registered with the State Bar of California and has a currently effective certificate of registration from the State Bar pursuant to the Professional Corporation Act ... and this article," and identifies the State Bar as "the governmental agency" Moscone-Knox itself refers to for a law corporation. Filing articles with the Secretary of State creates the corporation as a legal entity; obtaining and maintaining the certificate of registration from the profession's own regulating agency is what actually authorizes that corporation to render the licensed professional services in question, and the two steps are governed by different statutes and different state offices.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A professional corporation or a foreign professional corporation qualified to render professional services in this state shall be subject to the applicable rules and regulations adopted by, and all the disciplinary provisions of the Business and Professions Code expressly governing the practice of the profession in this state, and to the powers of, the governmental agency regulating the profession in which such corporation is engaged."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 13410(a), Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act, subjection to the regulating agency's rules, regulations, and disciplinary powers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=13410.)
  "A law corporation is a corporation which is registered with the State Bar of California and has a currently effective certificate of registration from the State Bar pursuant to the Professional Corporation Act, as contained in Part 4 (commencing with Section 13400) of Division 3 of Title 1 of the Corporations Code, and this article."
  — Bus. & Prof. Code § 6160, Law Corporations article, State Bar registration and certificate of registration as the Moscone-Knox regulating agency for law corporations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=6160.)

expectedJSON.body: Neither the Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act nor the profession-specific acts layered on top of it contain an express provision stating that a licensed professional's own liability for their own professional negligence disappears when they incorporate. Forming a professional corporation is understood, under general California corporate and agency principles, to shield a shareholder-professional from personal liability for the corporation's ordinary business debts and, in most circumstances, from liability for the malpractice of other shareholders or employees — but it does not extend that shield to a professional's liability for their own individually negligent or wrongful acts in rendering professional services, which remains a matter of personal responsibility regardless of the corporate form through which the services were rendered. Two profession-specific statutes in the Business and Professions Code supply indirect but real statutory evidence that this liability exposure persists notwithstanding incorporation: both the law corporation article and the accountancy corporation article condition the corporation's certificate of registration on the corporation maintaining insurance or other security for client claims arising out of the rendering of professional services — a mandatory-insurance condition that would serve no purpose if incorporating eliminated the underlying liability the insurance is meant to cover.

expectedJSON.body: A professional corporation is not governed by an entirely separate corporate-law regime. Cal. Corp. Code § 13403 states the relationship directly: "[t]he provisions of the General Corporation Law shall apply to professional corporations, except where such provisions are in conflict with or inconsistent with the provisions of this part." Consistent with that structure, Cal. Corp. Code § 13404 confirms that a professional corporation is formed the same way an ordinary corporation is formed — "under the General Corporation Law" — for the added purpose of qualifying as a professional corporation, with the one required deviation that its articles of incorporation "shall contain a specific statement that the corporation is a professional corporation within the meaning of this part." So a professional corporation exists on the same General Corporation Law chassis as an ordinary for-profit corporation, modified by the Moscone-Knox Act's own rules only where the two conflict — for example, Section 13403 itself goes on to supply special reduced-director rules for a professional corporation with only one or two shareholders, displacing what the General Corporation Law would otherwise require.

expectedJSON.body: Filing articles of incorporation with the California Secretary of State is not, by itself, enough to let a professional corporation render professional services. Cal. Corp. Code § 13410(a) subjects a professional corporation to the applicable rules, regulations, and disciplinary provisions of "the governmental agency regulating the profession in which such corporation is engaged" — the same licensing board that regulates individual practitioners of that profession, layered onto the corporation itself. A concrete, verified example of the two-step process this creates is the law corporation: Bus. & Prof. Code § 6160 defines a "law corporation" as one that "is registered with the State Bar of California and has a currently effective certificate of registration from the State Bar pursuant to the Professional Corporation Act ... and this article," and identifies the State Bar as "the governmental agency" Moscone-Knox itself refers to for a law corporation. Filing articles with the Secretary of State creates the corporation as a legal entity; obtaining and maintaining the certificate of registration from the profession's own regulating agency is what actually authorizes that corporation to render the licensed professional services in question, and the two steps are governed by different statutes and different state offices.
